answer.rationale: The finance mandate of 18% spend reduction combined with the low-cost vendor's qualifying quote creates a tight decision window with 14 days to contract expiry. memory_c2 demonstrates that switching to the low-cost vendor achieved sharp cost reduction with quick onboarding and accurate invoicing—this is the historical precedent most directly applicable. Verification of c2 will confirm those operational metrics held. However, the assembly line runs at 94% committed volume with no buffer, creating real delivery risk if switching introduces any friction. memory_c4 shows renegotiation recovered margin without narrowing scope, and memory_c6 shows multi-year commitments unlock further volume pricing—both suggest the incumbent could close the gap if engaged immediately. The constraint is time: with 14 days and no auto-renew, a negotiation cycle may not complete in time. Switching to the low-cost vendor meets the mandate immediately and has proven execution history. The downstream risk is that at 94% utilization, any onboarding friction or allocation surprise could strain committed delivery. Deferring (memory_c5) is not viable here—month-to-month continuity requires a contract in place. A second source (memory_c3) would consume the single decision allocation without closing the cost mandate. The intended action accepts the delivery risk as the lesser of available bad outcomes, conditional on c2 verification confirming the vendor's operational reliability.
